newsitem.title: FRANCE: French markets set for rocky pre-election road.
newsitem.headline: French markets set for rocky pre-election road.

text.p: An early French election, if called by President Jacques Chirac, would expose financial markets to a period of volatility, analysts said.
But a win for the ruling coalition would reinforce its ability to implement tough policies needed to meet the criteria for joining a single European currency, they added.
French newspapers including Le Monde reported Chirac would go on television on Monday to call a two-round parliamentary election on May 25-June 1 or June 1-8.

Amid apparently orchestrated leaks by pro-government politicians, Chirac's office was tight-lipped except to deny a report in the daily Le Monde that the president was planning a sharp shift towards free market economic policies.
French financial markets came under pressure late last week as talk of a cabinet reshuffle or an early election intensified.

Should an early election be called, the main risk for financial markets is that the centre-right coalition, committed to the euro, loses to a Socialist-led alliance that could have difficulty reconciling pro-European deficit-cutting policies with a desire to stimulate growth and reduce record unemployment, analysts said.
Some newspapers said an internal government note warned that the public deficit in 1997 could be well above Maastrict Treaty targets unless new savings measures were taken.
French 10-year bond yields were some 15 basis points lower than German yields at the beginning of last week but the differential had halved by Friday.
The franc hit its highest level against the mark since June 1993 at 3.3615 on Wednesday but slipped to 3.37 late on Friday as speculation about an early election mounted.
Analysts said a win for the centre-right coalition, even with a sharply reduced majority, would cause French markets to rebound to the levels reached early last week.

But a Socialist victory could considerably weaken the franc and cause a sharp rise in short-term interest rates until a new government managed to convince markets that it would do whatever is necessary to respect the criteria for joining a single currency, they said.

"If the left wins, then the new government will have to convince markets. Before that happens, targets could be 3.42 for the franc, 3.50 percent for the three-month rate," Dominique Barbet, bond analyst at Banque Paribas, said in a research note.
He said French 10-year government bond yields, currently eight basis points below German yields, could rise to 20 basis points above the yield on their German counterparts.
"In case of an early election, the challenge for both domestic and international investors is certainly to find the correct timing to buy on dips," Barbet said.

Economists at Credit Commercial de France said in a research note that a victory for a coalition made up the Socialists, Communists and Greens would leave President Jacques Chirac in a weak position both at home and abroad.
Although the Socialists support European monetary union, they could come under pressure from the anti-Maastrict Communists and might oppose any further reductions in government spending, they said.
"From the markets' point of view, a change in majority could be very negative for the franc and would lead to a divergence between French and German interest rates," they said.
Given the uncertainty which a snap poll announcement would unleash, analysts said French markets would be at the mercy of almost every opinion poll released until the outcome is known.
"This will put a lot of pressure on the French market, whose ups and downs will depend on the latest opinion polls, since so much rides on who wins the election," Barbet said.
Analysts at Union Europeene de CIC were said while an election would increase volatility, the overall French position on monetary union would probably remain little changed.
"Whatever happens politically in the near term, there is an overwhelmingly strong chance for us that France will remain firmly pro-EMU and on course for a three percent deficit in 1997," they said.
They said in a note to investors they believed the left would in fact be very pro-Europe once in power "but some investors may need time to be convinced."
Barbet at Paribas said a reshuffle, rather than an early election, would be positive for markets as it would confirm at worst a continuation of the current policy, or more likely, a tougher one.
Nevertheless, analysts at CIC said a reshuffle would do little to stop speculation about the outcome of elections which are still scheduled to take place in spring 1998.
((-- David Clarke, Paris Newsroom +331 4221 5542))
